Acceptable Evidence Includes:
- Screenshots of the internal wiki or documentation portal (e.g., Confluence, SharePoint, Google Drive, intranet site) showing where policies are stored.
- A table of contents or directory listing available policies.
- Access control settings confirming that all employees have read permissions.
- Screenshots of internal announcements (e.g., email, Slack, Teams messages) informing employees where policies are located.
- Screenshots of onboarding materials that direct new employees to the policy repository.
- Records of employee acknowledgments confirming they have accessed and reviewed policies.
Note: If this is handled within Vanta, simply "Add URL" to the [onboarding page](/employee/onboarding).

documents.description:
Provide evidence demonstrating that the production network is segregated from other environments (e.g., development, testing, corporate networks).
Acceptable evidence can include:
- A network topology diagram showing how production, development, and other environments are separated.
- Labels identifying firewalls, VLANs, subnets, DMZs, and restricted access controls.
- Screenshots of firewall rules, security groups, or network ACLs that enforce segregation between production and non-production environments.
- Screenshots or configurations showing Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), Security Groups, and Network ACLs in AWS, Azure, or GCP.
- Subnet configurations demonstrating that production workloads are isolated within private subnets.
- Routing tables confirming restricted access between production and non-production environments.
- Evidence of Virtual Network Peering or AWS PrivateLink enforcing private, internal-only communication.
- Logs from SIEM, firewalls, or cloud security tools showing restricted traffic flow between production and other networks.
A template can be found here: [Google docs template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1q_7KCd0KKwfY3n7JOYfMIDYYdUbsEcoL75MHYd5kTMs/copy)

documents.title: Secure configuration baselines developed
documents.description:
Provide evidence of documented configuration baselines based on industry standards such as CIS, NIST 800 series, NIST STIGs, etc.) for all in-scope systems such as:
1. Operating Systems
2. Cloud Infrastructure and Services
3. Servers or Compute Instances
4. Endpoint Software
5. Network Infrastructure (Firewalls, VPCs, Security Groups)
6. Databases
Acceptable evidence can include:
- A configuration baseline document outlining security settings for each in-scope system.
- Screenshots or reports from security tools (e.g., CIS Benchmark scans, AWS Security Hub findings) showing compliance with baseline standards.
- Documentation of access controls, logging configurations, and system monitoring settings.
- A simple spreadsheet listing key configurations and security settings applied across systems.
Implementation Guidance for Startups:
If you don’t have a mature IT team, start with these steps:
- Identify what you use – List the technologies you rely on (e.g., AWS, Linux, Windows, databases, firewalls).
- Use existing templates – Download CIS benchmarks or NIST STIGs relevant to your technology stack. Many security tools (e.g., AWS Security Hub, Microsoft Defender) provide default recommendations.
- Apply basic hardening – Disable unnecessary services, enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA), enable logging, and restrict admin access.
- Document in a simple format – A Google Doc or spreadsheet listing key security settings is enough to start. Track what’s configured, who owns it, and when it was last reviewed.
- Set up alerts & reviews – Use built-in cloud security tools (AWS Config, Azure Security Center) to monitor compliance, and schedule periodic checks (quarterly or biannually) to keep settings up to date.
Audit Consideration: During your audit window, be prepared to re-upload evidence for at least a 10% for your interconnected system components, as randomly selected and requested by your auditor.
A template can be found here: [Google docs template](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1omSk3wxiZKWuYGGZlBqyNWtETUw1dT-3YwoVimOatMg/copy)

documents.title: Web Filtering Capabilities
documents.description:
Provide evidence that demonstrates that your organization has implemented web filtering controls to reduce the risk of personnel accessing websites that contain illegal content, viruses, or phishing materials. This includes blocking access to known or suspected malicious websites, command and control servers, and websites sharing illegal content.
Where to find the web filtering evidence:
1) Web Protection in Anti-malware Solutions: Many small businesses already use anti-malware or antivirus software that includes basic web filtering features. If the company has an Anti-malware Solution, it likely has built-in Web Protection or Web Filtering.
Where to check:
Open the anti-malware software dashboard.
Look for sections like Web Protection, Safe Browsing, or Web Control. This will typically list blocked websites or threats encountered during browsing.
Capture screenshots of the enabled web filtering settings or download a report from the software.
2) Firewall or Router Settings: If the company uses a business-grade firewall or router (e.g., Cisco, SonicWall, or even certain Netgear routers), web filtering can often be configured directly within these devices.
Where to check:
Access the firewall or router’s admin panel.
Look for sections like URL Filtering, Content Filtering, or Web Filtering.
Capture screenshots of the settings and any activity logs showing blocked website attempts.
3) Browser-Based Protections: Modern browsers (like Chrome, Firefox, and Edge) come with built-in protection against dangerous websites.
Where to check:
In Chrome, go to Settings > Privacy and Security > Security. Check for “Safe Browsing” settings.
Capture screenshots of this setting enabled.

documents.title: Network diagram
documents.description:
Provide a detailed network diagram.
Guidance: A proper network diagram consists of several key components and attributes, such as:
1. Boundary Definitions with clear demarcation of network boundaries, such as firewalls, routers, gateways, and VPNs
2. Network Devices listed such as servers, switches, bastion servers, routers, firewalls, and IDS/IPS systems with clear labels 
3. Subnets within the network and their boundaries
4. Representation of data flows in the network and the type of entity involved in the flow (e.g., public, private customer, internal employee, internal host, etc)
5. Network zones such as public, private, DMZ, or other specific zones like cardholder data environments for PCI DSS.
6. Security controls in use within the network architecture such as firewalls, IDS/IPS systems, NAC systems, web application firewalls, etc.
7. Critical system inclusion such as identifying key databases, servers, cryptographic servers, etc.
8. Physical locations of network components (e.g., AWS US-East)
9. Redundancy and failover mechanisms such as network load balancers and disaster recovery locations
A template can be found here: [Google docs template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1FOOjO1ZYwWsc7CM25S0CQ-XrQirov7WvE6Zs8UEuYiU/copy)

documents.title: Penetration test remediation
documents.description:
Provide evidence demonstrating that issues identified during your most recent periodic penetration test have been addressed.​
Acceptable evidence and implementation guidance:
- Remediation Documentation: Submit records such as tickets, reports, or logs that detail the identified issues, assigned personnel, remediation steps, and current status.​
- Follow-up Testing Reports: Results from subsequent tests confirming that previously identified vulnerabilities have been effectively addressed.​
- Management Sign-off: Approvals from leadership acknowledging the completion and effectiveness of remediation efforts.
- Configuration Changes: Logs or records detailing modifications to system configurations to mitigate identified risks.
- Patch Management Records: Evidence of applied patches or updates to address vulnerabilities found during the penetration test.
If no issues were found, provide documentation such as meeting minutes or internal communications confirming the review and acknowledgment of the penetration test results.

documents.title: Security integration tests
documents.description:
Provide evidence demonstrating the implementation of automated security testing within your application or infrastructure, including Static Application Security Testing (SAST), Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), and Software Composition Analysis (SCA).​
Acceptable evidence and implementation guidance:
- Documentation of Security Testing Procedures: Outline your organization's approach to integrating automated security tests, specifying the tools used (e.g., GitHub Advanced Security, OWASP ZAP) and the frequency of these tests.​
- Sample Security Test Reports: Provide recent reports from SAST, DAST, or SCA tools that detail identified vulnerabilities and the steps taken to address them.​
- CI/CD Pipeline Integration Evidence: Show how security testing tools are incorporated into your continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline, ensuring that code is automatically scanned for vulnerabilities during development.​
- Access to Security Dashboards: Offer access to dashboards or platforms where ongoing security testing results are displayed, demonstrating continuous monitoring and management of security risks.​
- Training Records: Document training sessions or materials provided to development teams on the importance and implementation of automated security testing practices.
